meanings: to have (used for people and animals)
to put on from the shoulders down
to take a photo or record a film
to make a sound (of an animal)
I am glad to meet you
to play an instrument with strings

grammar.title: A は B です
grammar.explanation:
は marks the topic; です politely identifies or describes it. は is pronounced wa as a particle.

Formation: Noun A + は + noun B + です. For a negative identification use Bではありません; the polite past is Bでした.

Usage and cautions: Use this pattern to establish what the topic is, not what action it performs. は is written ha but pronounced wa. Japanese often omits an already understood topic; repeating 私は in every sentence is unnecessary. Do not add です directly to a dictionary-form verb.

examples.ja: 私は学生です。
examples.en: I am a student.

examples.ja: 父は医者です。
examples.reading: ちちはいしゃです。
examples.en: My father is a doctor.

examples.ja: 昨日は休みでした。
examples.reading: きのうはやすみでした。
examples.en: Yesterday was a day off.

questions.prompt: Choose the topic marker: 私＿学生です。
questions.explanation: The correct answer is “は”. は presents 私 as the topic; を marks an object and で usually marks a setting or means.

questions.prompt: Say politely “I was a teacher”: 私は先生＿。
questions.explanation: でした is the past copula: the speaker was a teacher. です is nonpast and ではありません is negative.

questions.prompt: Say politely “This is not a hospital”: ここは病院＿。
questions.explanation: Noun + ではありません politely denies identification; います describes animate existence, not identity.

questions.prompt: Choose the best English meaning: 父は医者です。
questions.explanation: “父は医者です。” means “My father is a doctor.” in this example. Use this pattern to establish what the topic is, not what action it performs.

questions.prompt: Choose the best English meaning: 昨日は休みでした。
choices: Yesterday was not a day off.
I take a break every day.
questions.explanation: “昨日は休みでした。” means “Yesterday was a day off.” in this example. Use this pattern to establish what the topic is, not what action it performs.

grammar.title: Questions with か
grammar.explanation:
Add か to a polite sentence to ask a question. Japanese does not require English-style subject–verb inversion.

Formation: Polite statement + か. Question words such as 何 and どこ remain in the position where their answer would go.

Usage and cautions: A polite question needs no change of word order. In writing, か can take a full stop. Bare plain-form questions with か can sound blunt, so use ですか or ますか with unfamiliar people. Answer the intended proposition rather than translating English yes/no mechanically.

examples.ja: 田中さんは先生ですか。
examples.en: Is Tanaka a teacher?

examples.ja: これは何ですか。
examples.reading: これはなんですか。
examples.en: What is this?

examples.ja: 明日、働きますか。
examples.reading: あした、はたらきますか。
examples.en: Will you work tomorrow?

questions.prompt: Complete a polite question: 学生です＿。
questions.explanation: The correct answer is “か”. Sentence-final か turns the polite statement into a question.

questions.prompt: Ask politely “Where is the station?”: 駅はどこです＿。
questions.explanation: Sentence-final か makes どこです a polite question; the other particles cannot perform that function.

questions.prompt: Which sentence asks whether someone ate breakfast?
choices: 朝ご飯を食べましょう。
朝ご飯を食べましたか。
questions.explanation: Past polite 食べました plus か asks about a completed meal; the other sentences state, deny or suggest eating.

questions.prompt: Choose the best English meaning: これは何ですか。
questions.explanation: “これは何ですか。” means “What is this?” in this example. A polite question needs no change of word order.

questions.prompt: Choose the best English meaning: 明日、働きますか。
questions.explanation: “明日、働きますか。” means “Will you work tomorrow?” in this example. A polite question needs no change of word order.

grammar.title: Possession with の
grammar.explanation:
Connect two nouns with の to express ownership, association, or specification. The noun being described comes last.

Formation: Possessor or specifying noun + の + head noun. A second の can stand for an understood possessed item: 私のです.

Usage and cautions: The final noun determines what the whole phrase refers to. の also marks affiliation or material-related association, not just legal ownership. Do not reverse the nouns by copying English word order, and do not use の as the ordinary connector after a な-adjective.

examples.ja: これは姉の本です。
examples.en: This is my older sister's book.

examples.ja: これは学校の図書館です。
examples.reading: これはがっこうのとしょかんです。
examples.en: This is the school library.

examples.ja: その傘は私のです。
examples.reading: そのかさはわたしのです。
examples.en: That umbrella is mine.

questions.prompt: Choose 'my book'.
questions.explanation: The correct answer is “私の本”. The possessor comes before の and the possessed noun after it.

questions.prompt: Choose “a Japanese-language teacher”.
questions.explanation: 日本語 specifies the kind of 先生, so it precedes の; 先生の日本語 would mean the teacher’s Japanese.

questions.prompt: Complete “my younger brother’s bicycle”: 弟＿自転車。
questions.explanation: 弟 is the possessor and 自転車 the possessed object; connect the two nouns with の.

questions.prompt: Choose the best English meaning: これは学校の図書館です。
choices: The school is inside my library.
questions.explanation: “これは学校の図書館です。” means “This is the school library.” in this example. The final noun determines what the whole phrase refers to.

questions.prompt: Choose the best English meaning: その傘は私のです。
questions.explanation: “その傘は私のです。” means “That umbrella is mine.” in this example. The final noun determines what the whole phrase refers to.

grammar.title: これ・それ・あれ
grammar.explanation:
これ refers to something near the speaker, それ near the listener, and あれ away from both. These stand alone; この etc. precede nouns.

Formation: これ・それ・あれ stand alone. この・その・あの must precede a noun. どれ / どの ask which one.

Usage and cautions: Choose the series by conversational distance: speaker, listener, or neither. それ can also refer back to something the other person mentioned. Do not attach a noun directly to これ, and do not confuse object words with location words ここ・そこ・あそこ.

examples.ja: それは何ですか。
examples.en: What is that near you?

examples.ja: このかばんは軽いです。
examples.reading: このかばんはかるいです。
examples.en: This bag is light.

examples.ja: あれは山田さんの車です。
examples.reading: あれはやまださんのくるまです。
examples.en: That over there is Yamada’s car.

questions.prompt: Which expression means 'this book'?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is “この本”. この modifies a following noun; これ itself means 'this thing'.

questions.prompt: A pen is in your listener’s hand. Say “that pen”: ＿ペン。
questions.explanation: その modifies ペン and points to something near the listener; これ and あれ stand alone, and ここ names a place.

questions.prompt: Point to one of three unclaimed bags and ask “Which is yours?”: ＿があなたのですか。
questions.explanation: どれ stands for an object by itself; どの needs a following noun, while どこ asks about a place.

questions.prompt: Choose the best English meaning: このかばんは軽いです。
questions.explanation: “このかばんは軽いです。” means “This bag is light.” in this example. Choose the series by conversational distance: speaker, listener, or neither.

questions.prompt: Choose the best English meaning: あれは山田さんの車です。
choices: That over there is Yamada’s car.
This car beside me is Yamada’s.
questions.explanation: “あれは山田さんの車です。” means “That over there is Yamada’s car.” in this example. Choose the series by conversational distance: speaker, listener, or neither.

grammar.title: Object particle を
grammar.explanation:
を marks the direct object of an action. It is usually pronounced o, not wo, in modern Japanese.

Formation: Action target + を + transitive verb. を is pronounced o. Certain movement verbs also mark a route with を.

Usage and cautions: The direct object is the thing affected, consumed, read or watched. In ordinary beginner sentences the action location takes で instead. Existence verbs ある and いる do not take を for the entity that exists; use が. The object can be omitted when understood.

examples.ja: 水を飲みます。
examples.en: I drink water.

examples.ja: 毎朝、新聞を読みます。
examples.reading: まいあさ、しんぶんをよみます。
examples.en: I read the newspaper every morning.

examples.ja: 昨日、映画を見ました。
examples.reading: きのう、えいがをみました。
examples.en: I watched a film yesterday.

questions.prompt: Complete: パン＿食べます。
questions.explanation: The correct answer is “を”. パン is the thing being eaten, so it takes を.

questions.prompt: Mark the thing bought: 駅で切符＿買いました。
questions.explanation: 切符 is the purchased object and takes を; 駅で already supplies the location of buying.

questions.prompt: Choose “I listen to music”.
questions.explanation: 聞く takes the thing deliberately listened to with を; the alternatives do not express this intended action.

questions.prompt: Choose the best English meaning: 毎朝、新聞を読みます。
choices: I read the newspaper every morning.
I write a newspaper every night.
questions.explanation: “毎朝、新聞を読みます。” means “I read the newspaper every morning.” in this example. The direct object is the thing affected, consumed, read or watched.

questions.prompt: Choose the best English meaning: 昨日、映画を見ました。
choices: I will watch a film tomorrow.
I did not watch a film yesterday.
questions.explanation: “昨日、映画を見ました。” means “I watched a film yesterday.” in this example. The direct object is the thing affected, consumed, read or watched.

grammar.source: Original curriculum; CC BY-SA 4.0. Level placement is an estimate, not an official JLPT syllabus.

grammar.title: Action location で
grammar.explanation:
Use で for the place where an activity occurs. に is used for an existence location or destination instead.

Formation: Place + で + activity verb. Means or tools can also take で: バスで, ペンで.

Usage and cautions: で answers where an activity is carried out. A destination with 行く uses に or へ; the location of existence with ある or いる normally uses に. Do not choose a particle just from English “at”: first identify the Japanese predicate.

examples.ja: 図書館で勉強します。
examples.en: I study at the library.

examples.ja: 家で昼ご飯を食べます。
examples.reading: いえでひるごはんをたべます。
examples.en: I eat lunch at home.

examples.ja: 公園で友達と話しました。
examples.reading: こうえんでともだちとはなしました。
examples.en: I talked with a friend in the park.

questions.prompt: Where does the action happen? 学校＿勉強します。
questions.explanation: The correct answer is “で”. Studying is an activity, so its location is marked by で.

questions.prompt: The activity is swimming at a pool: プール＿泳ぎます。
questions.explanation: The pool is the setting of the swimming activity, so use で rather than a destination particle.

questions.prompt: Contrast activity and existence: 教室＿先生がいます。
questions.explanation: います expresses existence; its location takes に, even though activity locations in this lesson take で.

questions.prompt: Choose the best English meaning: 家で昼ご飯を食べます。
choices: I do not eat at home.
questions.explanation: “家で昼ご飯を食べます。” means “I eat lunch at home.” in this example. で answers where an activity is carried out.

questions.prompt: Choose the best English meaning: 公園で友達と話しました。
choices: I walked to my friend’s park.
My friend lives in the park.
I will talk alone at home.
I talked with a friend in the park.
questions.explanation: “公園で友達と話しました。” means “I talked with a friend in the park.” in this example. で answers where an activity is carried out.

grammar.source: Original curriculum; CC BY-SA 4.0. Level placement is an estimate, not an official JLPT syllabus.

grammar.title: Destination に・へ
grammar.explanation:
に marks a destination; へ emphasizes direction and is pronounced e. Either can accompany 行く, 来る, or 帰る.

Formation: Destination + に / へ + 行く・来る・帰る. A purpose may follow a verb stem: 買いに行く.

Usage and cautions: に presents an arrival point; へ emphasizes movement toward a direction and is pronounced e. Either often works, so exercises must not present them as mutually exclusive in a neutral travel sentence. で instead marks the means of travel, such as 電車で.

examples.ja: 明日、東京に行きます。
examples.en: I am going to Tokyo tomorrow.

examples.ja: 週末、海へ行きます。
examples.reading: しゅうまつ、うみへいきます。
examples.en: I will go to the sea this weekend.

examples.ja: 母は六時に家に帰ります。
examples.reading: はははろくじにいえにかえります。
examples.en: My mother returns home at six.

questions.prompt: Choose a destination particle: 日本＿行きます。
questions.explanation: The correct answer is “に”. に identifies the destination. へ would also work, but を and が do not express it here.

questions.prompt: Select the destination expression: 日曜日、京都＿旅行します。
questions.explanation: 京都へ expresses the direction of the trip; the alternatives here do not mark Kyoto as its destination.

questions.prompt: Mark the means, not the destination: バス＿学校に行きます。
questions.explanation: バスで states how one travels; 学校に already identifies the destination.

questions.prompt: Choose the best English meaning: 週末、海へ行きます。
choices: I work at sea every day.
I came from the sea yesterday.
I will not go out this weekend.
I will go to the sea this weekend.
questions.explanation: “週末、海へ行きます。” means “I will go to the sea this weekend.” in this example. に presents an arrival point; へ emphasizes movement toward a direction and is pronounced e.

questions.prompt: Choose the best English meaning: 母は六時に家に帰ります。
choices: My mother stays at the station until six.
My mother returns home at six.
My mother leaves home at six.
questions.explanation: “母は六時に家に帰ります。” means “My mother returns home at six.” in this example. に presents an arrival point; へ emphasizes movement toward a direction and is pronounced e.

grammar.source: Original curriculum; CC BY-SA 4.0. Level placement is an estimate, not an official JLPT syllabus.

grammar.title: Existence: ある・いる
grammar.explanation:
Use ある for inanimate things and いる for people and animals. Mark the existence location with に and the entity with が.

Formation: Place に + entity が + ある / いる. Polite forms: あります / います; negatives: ありません / いません.

Usage and cautions: Use いる for people and animals, and ある for objects and plants. With a topic, Xはplaceにあります describes where X is. The negative of ある in plain speech is ない, not あらない. Do not mark the existence location with activity particle で.

examples.ja: 庭に猫がいます。
examples.en: There is a cat in the garden.

examples.ja: 机の上に本があります。
examples.reading: つくえのうえにほんがあります。
examples.en: There is a book on the desk.

examples.ja: 部屋に誰もいません。
examples.reading: へやにだれもいません。
examples.en: There is nobody in the room.

questions.prompt: Complete the existence sentence for a dog: 犬が＿。
questions.explanation: The correct answer is “います”. Dogs are animate, so use いる, politely います.

questions.prompt: Choose existence for a tree: 庭に大きな木が＿。
questions.explanation: Trees take ある despite being living organisms; Japanese uses いる for animate people and animals.

questions.prompt: Choose the negative for people: 今日は事務所に社員が＿。
questions.explanation: 社員 are people, so negative existence is いません; ではありません would deny an identity.

questions.prompt: Choose the best English meaning: 机の上に本があります。
choices: The desk is inside the book.
There are no books on the desk.
There is a book on the desk.
A person is reading under the desk.
questions.explanation: “机の上に本があります。” means “There is a book on the desk.” in this example. Use いる for people and animals, and ある for objects and plants.

questions.prompt: Choose the best English meaning: 部屋に誰もいません。
choices: There is nobody in the room.
There is no furniture in the room.
questions.explanation: “部屋に誰もいません。” means “There is nobody in the room.” in this example. Use いる for people and animals, and ある for objects and plants.

grammar.source: Original curriculum; CC BY-SA 4.0. Level placement is an estimate, not an official JLPT syllabus.

grammar.title: Polite verb forms
grammar.explanation:
The ます form is polite nonpast: present habits or future actions. ません is negative, ました past, and ませんでした past negative.

Formation: Verb stem + ます / ません / ました / ませんでした. The stem varies by verb class: 書き-, 食べ-, し-, 来（き）-.

Usage and cautions: Nonpast ます covers habits and future events; context supplies the time. Past negative retains ません before でした. Politeness is not the same as tense. Do not combine ます with です, or create a past by appending た directly to ます.

examples.ja: 昨日、働きませんでした。
examples.en: I did not work yesterday.

examples.ja: 毎日、駅まで歩きます。
examples.reading: まいにち、えきまであるきます。
examples.en: I walk to the station every day.

examples.ja: 明日は働きません。
examples.reading: あしたははたらきません。
examples.en: I will not work tomorrow.

questions.prompt: Choose the polite past of 食べます.
questions.explanation: The correct answer is “食べました”. ました expresses a completed past action; ません is nonpast negative.

questions.prompt: Say politely “I did not read it yesterday”: 昨日、読み＿。
questions.explanation: ませんでした is the polite past negative; ませんです is not the standard inflection.

questions.prompt: Say “I will come tomorrow” politely: 明日、来＿。
questions.explanation: 来ます is polite nonpast and can describe tomorrow; ますです incorrectly stacks polite endings.

questions.prompt: Choose the best English meaning: 毎日、駅まで歩きます。
choices: I am waiting at the station.
I walk to the station every day.
I walked to the station only yesterday.
I never walk to the station.
questions.explanation: “毎日、駅まで歩きます。” means “I walk to the station every day.” in this example. Nonpast ます covers habits and future events; context supplies the time.

questions.prompt: Choose the best English meaning: 明日は働きません。
questions.explanation: “明日は働きません。” means “I will not work tomorrow.” in this example. Nonpast ます covers habits and future events; context supplies the time.

grammar.source: Original curriculum; CC BY-SA 4.0. Level placement is an estimate, not an official JLPT syllabus.

grammar.title: い-adjective inflection
grammar.explanation:
For an い-adjective, replace final い with くない for negative or かった for past. いい has the forms よくない and よかった.

Formation: Final い → くない (negative), かった (past), くなかった (past negative). Add です for a polite adjective predicate.

Usage and cautions: Only the final inflectional い changes. いい uses よ- in inflected forms: よくない, よかった. An い-adjective directly modifies a noun without な. Words such as きれい are な-adjectives even though their spelling ends in い.

examples.ja: 昨日は寒かったです。
examples.en: It was cold yesterday.

examples.ja: この部屋は広くないです。
examples.reading: このへやはひろくないです。
examples.en: This room is not spacious.

examples.ja: 昨日の試験は難しくなかったです。
examples.reading: きのうのしけんはむずかしくなかったです。
examples.en: Yesterday’s exam was not difficult.

questions.prompt: Choose the negative of 高い.
questions.explanation: The correct answer is “高くない”. Remove final い and add くない. 高かった is past affirmative.

questions.prompt: Choose the past affirmative of いい.
questions.explanation: いい exceptionally uses the stem よ-; the past is よかった, not いかった or いいでした.

questions.prompt: Complete “a cheap shop”: 安＿店。
questions.explanation: 安い directly precedes a noun; adding な is incorrect for an い-adjective.

questions.prompt: Choose the best English meaning: この部屋は広くないです。
questions.explanation: “この部屋は広くないです。” means “This room is not spacious.” in this example. Only the final inflectional い changes.

questions.prompt: Choose the best English meaning: 昨日の試験は難しくなかったです。
choices: I did not take yesterday’s exam.
questions.explanation: “昨日の試験は難しくなかったです。” means “Yesterday’s exam was not difficult.” in this example. Only the final inflectional い changes.

grammar.source: Original curriculum; CC BY-SA 4.0. Level placement is an estimate, not an official JLPT syllabus.

grammar.title: な-adjectives before nouns
grammar.explanation:
A な-adjective takes な before a noun, but not before です. Many adjectives ending in a written い, such as きれい, belong here.

Formation: な-adjective + な + noun; at the end of a polite sentence use adjective + です. Plain negative: ではない.

Usage and cautions: The な links the adjective to its noun; it is not retained before です. Common members include 静か, 便利, 元気 and きれい. Do not classify adjectives solely by their last written character: きれい and 有名 are both な-adjectives.

examples.ja: 静かな町です。
examples.en: It is a quiet town.

examples.ja: ここは便利な駅です。
examples.reading: ここはべんりなえきです。
examples.en: This is a convenient station.

examples.ja: この町は静かではありません。
examples.reading: このまちはしずかではありません。
examples.en: This town is not quiet.

questions.prompt: Complete: きれい＿花です。
questions.explanation: The correct answer is “な”. きれい is a な-adjective, so it links to 花 with な.

questions.prompt: Complete the polite predicate: この部屋はきれい＿。
questions.explanation: きれい is a な-adjective; before です use the bare adjective, not きれいなです or an い-adjective ending.

questions.prompt: Choose “a famous person”.
questions.explanation: A な-adjective needs な immediately before its noun: 有名な人.

questions.prompt: Choose the best English meaning: ここは便利な駅です。
questions.explanation: “ここは便利な駅です。” means “This is a convenient station.” in this example. The な links the adjective to its noun; it is not retained before です.

questions.prompt: Choose the best English meaning: この町は静かではありません。
choices: This town used to be quiet.
questions.explanation: “この町は静かではありません。” means “This town is not quiet.” in this example. The な links the adjective to its noun; it is not retained before です.

grammar.source: Original curriculum; CC BY-SA 4.0. Level placement is an estimate, not an official JLPT syllabus.

grammar.title: Time expressions with に
grammar.explanation:
Use に after a specific clock time or date to mark when an event occurs. Relative words such as 今日 and 明日 normally do not need it.

Formation: Specific clock time or date + に + event. 毎日, 今日, 昨日 and 明日 usually appear without に.

Usage and cautions: Use に for a scheduled point in time, not automatically for every time expression. Durations such as 三時間 are different from clock times such as 三時. Approximate times can use ごろ, often without に. A weekday may take に when locating an event.

examples.ja: 七時に起きます。
examples.en: I get up at seven.

examples.ja: 月曜日に試験があります。
examples.reading: げつようびにしけんがあります。
examples.en: There is an exam on Monday.

examples.ja: 明日、友達に会います。
examples.reading: あした、ともだちにあいます。
examples.en: I will meet a friend tomorrow.

questions.prompt: Complete: 九時＿寝ます。
questions.explanation: The correct answer is “に”. A specific clock time uses に.

questions.prompt: Complete a specific clock time: 会議は二時＿始まります。
questions.explanation: 二時 is the scheduled time when the meeting starts, so use に.

questions.prompt: Which normally needs no time particle に?
questions.explanation: Relative 今日 normally stands alone; the other expressions can take に to specify when an event occurs.

questions.prompt: Choose the best English meaning: 月曜日に試験があります。
choices: There was an exam last Monday.
There is no exam on Monday.
There is an exam on Monday.
questions.explanation: “月曜日に試験があります。” means “There is an exam on Monday.” in this example. Use に for a scheduled point in time, not automatically for every time expression.

questions.prompt: Choose the best English meaning: 明日、友達に会います。
choices: I will meet a friend tomorrow.
I see my friend every day.
questions.explanation: “明日、友達に会います。” means “I will meet a friend tomorrow.” in this example. Use に for a scheduled point in time, not automatically for every time expression.

grammar.source: Original curriculum; CC BY-SA 4.0. Level placement is an estimate, not an official JLPT syllabus.

grammar.title: Invitation: ませんか
grammar.explanation:
A negative polite question can invite someone to do something together. ましょう suggests or agrees to a shared action.

Formation: Verb ます-stem + ませんか invites; stem + ましょう suggests a shared action or accepts an invitation.

Usage and cautions: The negative question leaves room for the listener to decline. Distinguish an invitation from a factual question by context. ましょう can sound more decisive because it assumes a shared action. These patterns invite action rather than describing past activity.

examples.ja: 一緒に映画を見ませんか。
examples.en: Would you like to watch a film together?

examples.ja: 一緒に昼ご飯を食べませんか。
examples.reading: いっしょにひるごはんをたべませんか。
examples.en: Would you like to have lunch together?

examples.ja: 少し休みましょう。
examples.reading: すこしやすみましょう。
examples.en: Let’s take a short break.

questions.prompt: Choose a polite invitation.
choices: お茶を飲みませんでした
questions.explanation: The correct answer is “お茶を飲みませんか”. ませんか invites; the other options report past events.

questions.prompt: Invite someone to go to a park: 公園に行き＿。
questions.explanation: 行きませんか is an invitation in this shared-outing context; the other endings do not invite.

questions.prompt: Accept a suggestion to walk: はい、歩き＿。
questions.explanation: ましょう expresses willing agreement to the proposed shared walk, not a past event.

questions.prompt: Choose the best English meaning: 一緒に昼ご飯を食べませんか。
choices: Would you like to have lunch together?
Did you already eat lunch alone?
Do not eat lunch with me.
questions.explanation: “一緒に昼ご飯を食べませんか。” means “Would you like to have lunch together?” in this example. The negative question leaves room for the listener to decline.

questions.prompt: Choose the best English meaning: 少し休みましょう。
choices: You must not take a break.
questions.explanation: “少し休みましょう。” means “Let’s take a short break.” in this example. The negative question leaves room for the listener to decline.

grammar.title: Requests with てください
grammar.explanation:
The verb て-form followed by ください makes a polite request. It can still sound directive, so use care with superiors.

Formation: Verb て-form + ください. Godan changes include 書いて, 飲んで, 待って; する → して, 来る → 来て.

Usage and cautions: Use this to request a concrete action. A request can still be an instruction, so more indirect forms may suit a superior or a favor. To request non-action use ないでください; なくてください is not the standard negative request.

examples.ja: ここに名前を書いてください。
examples.en: Please write your name here.

examples.ja: 窓を開けてください。
examples.reading: まどをあけてください。
examples.en: Please open the window.

examples.ja: ここで写真を撮らないでください。
examples.reading: ここでしゃしんをとらないでください。
examples.en: Please do not take photos here.

questions.prompt: Choose a request to wait.
questions.explanation: The correct answer is “待ってください”. The て-form 待って plus ください requests the action.

questions.prompt: Request reading aloud: 大きな声で読ん＿ください。
questions.explanation: 読む has the て-form 読んで, so the missing ending is で; 読んて is incorrect.

questions.prompt: Choose a request not to enter.
questions.explanation: Negative requests use the ない-form plus でください: 入らないでください.

questions.prompt: Choose the best English meaning: 窓を開けてください。
questions.explanation: “窓を開けてください。” means “Please open the window.” in this example. Use this to request a concrete action.

questions.prompt: Choose the best English meaning: ここで写真を撮らないでください。
choices: You do not need to take photos here.
Please do not take photos here.
questions.explanation: “ここで写真を撮らないでください。” means “Please do not take photos here.” in this example. Use this to request a concrete action.

grammar.title: Permission: てもいい
grammar.explanation:
Attach もいい to the て-form to say something is permitted. Add ですか to ask permission.

Formation: Verb て-form + もいい（です） permits an action; add か to ask permission. Negative なくてもいい permits non-action.

Usage and cautions: This asks whether an action is allowed, not whether the listener can perform it. Granting permission can imply authority; avoid casually approving a superior’s behavior. A prohibition is てはいけない, not the negative of a permission question.

examples.ja: ここに座ってもいいですか。
examples.en: May I sit here?

examples.ja: この辞書を使ってもいいです。
examples.reading: このじしょをつかってもいいです。
examples.en: You may use this dictionary.

examples.ja: 今日は早く帰ってもいいですか。
examples.reading: きょうははやくかえってもいいですか。
examples.en: May I go home early today?

questions.prompt: Which asks permission to take a photo?
choices: 写真を撮ってもいいですか
写真を撮りませんでした
questions.explanation: The correct answer is “写真を撮ってもいいですか”. てもいいですか asks whether doing the action is allowed.

questions.prompt: Ask permission to enter: 入っ＿いいですか。
questions.explanation: 入る becomes 入って; adding もいいですか asks whether entering is permitted.

questions.prompt: Which grants permission to sit?
choices: 座らなければなりません。
questions.explanation: 座ってもいい grants permission; the alternatives request non-action, impose obligation or state inability.

questions.prompt: Choose the best English meaning: この辞書を使ってもいいです。
choices: This dictionary is easy to use.
questions.explanation: “この辞書を使ってもいいです。” means “You may use this dictionary.” in this example. This asks whether an action is allowed, not whether the listener can perform it.

questions.prompt: Choose the best English meaning: 今日は早く帰ってもいいですか。
choices: May I go home early today?
Did you come home early today?
questions.explanation: “今日は早く帰ってもいいですか。” means “May I go home early today?” in this example. This asks whether an action is allowed, not whether the listener can perform it.

grammar.title: Ongoing actions: ている
grammar.explanation:
The て-form plus いる describes an ongoing action. Some verbs instead express a resulting state, such as 結婚している, 'be married'.

Formation: Verb て-form + いる / います. Negative: ていない; past: ていた / ていました.

Usage and cautions: Activity verbs often describe action in progress, while change-of-state verbs can describe a resulting state: ドアが開いている means the door is open. Repeated habits can also use ている. Do not assume every instance translates as English “is doing”.

examples.ja: 今、本を読んでいます。
examples.en: I am reading a book now.

examples.ja: 妹は今、寝ています。
examples.reading: いもうとはいま、ねています。
examples.en: My younger sister is sleeping now.

examples.ja: あの人は結婚しています。
examples.reading: あのひとはけっこんしています。
examples.en: That person is married.

questions.prompt: Choose 'is eating now'.
choices: 今、食べないでください
questions.explanation: The correct answer is “今、食べています”. ている expresses the action in progress here, not a finished or negated past action.

questions.prompt: Describe ongoing rain: 今、雨が降っ＿。
questions.explanation: 降っています describes the rain currently in progress; the past forms do not express that ongoing state.

questions.prompt: In 窓が開いています, what does ている describe?
questions.explanation: 開く is a change-of-state verb; 開いている normally describes the resulting state, “is open”.

questions.prompt: Choose the best English meaning: 妹は今、寝ています。
choices: My younger sister is sleeping now.
My younger sister will go to bed tomorrow.
questions.explanation: “妹は今、寝ています。” means “My younger sister is sleeping now.” in this example. Activity verbs often describe action in progress, while change-of-state verbs can describe a resulting state: ドアが開いている means the door is open.

questions.prompt: Choose the best English meaning: あの人は結婚しています。
choices: That person wants to get married.
That person is having a wedding right now.
questions.explanation: “あの人は結婚しています。” means “That person is married.” in this example. Activity verbs often describe action in progress, while change-of-state verbs can describe a resulting state: ドアが開いている means the door is open.

grammar.title: Desire: たい
grammar.explanation:
Attach たい to the verb's ます-stem to express your desire to act. It inflects like an い-adjective. Avoid directly assuming strangers' private desires.

Formation: Verb ます-stem + たい. Negative たくない; past たかった; past negative たくなかった.

Usage and cautions: たい behaves like an い-adjective and expresses the speaker’s own desire, or asks the listener’s. For an observed third-person desire, たがっている is useful. Objects may take を or が. Do not add たい to the dictionary form or mistake a wish for a fixed plan.

examples.ja: 日本に行きたいです。
examples.en: I want to go to Japan.

examples.ja: 今日は何も食べたくないです。
examples.reading: きょうはなにもたべたくないです。
examples.en: I do not want to eat anything today.

examples.ja: 子供のころ、先生になりたかったです。
examples.reading: こどものころ、せんせいになりたかったです。
examples.en: When I was a child, I wanted to become a teacher.

questions.prompt: Complete 'want to drink': 飲み＿。
questions.explanation: The correct answer is “たい”. 飲み is the ます-stem of 飲む; adding たい expresses desire.

questions.prompt: Choose “want to see”: 見＿。
questions.explanation: The stem of 見る is 見; attach たい directly to form 見たい.

questions.prompt: Choose the polite negative of 行きたい.
questions.explanation: たい inflects like an い-adjective: たい becomes たくない; たかった is past affirmative.

questions.prompt: Choose the best English meaning: 今日は何も食べたくないです。
choices: I wanted to eat everything today.
I do not want to eat anything today.
questions.explanation: “今日は何も食べたくないです。” means “I do not want to eat anything today.” in this example. たい behaves like an い-adjective and expresses the speaker’s own desire, or asks the listener’s.

questions.prompt: Choose the best English meaning: 子供のころ、先生になりたかったです。
choices: When I was a child, I wanted to become a teacher.
As a child, I was a teacher.
I do not want to be a teacher now.
My teacher wanted to become a child.
questions.explanation: “子供のころ、先生になりたかったです。” means “When I was a child, I wanted to become a teacher.” in this example. たい behaves like an い-adjective and expresses the speaker’s own desire, or asks the listener’s.

grammar.title: Reasons with から
grammar.explanation:
A clause ending in から gives a reason. The reason normally comes before the consequence; polite or plain clauses can precede から.

Formation: Reason clause + から、result. Nouns / な-adjectives use だから in plain speech or ですから politely.

Usage and cautions: から can give the speaker’s justification and can precede a request or decision. Keep the reason before the consequence in the basic pattern. Do not confuse reason から with starting-point から. With nouns, plain 雨から is not the usual reason clause; use 雨だから.

examples.ja: 雨ですから、出かけません。
examples.en: Because it is raining, I will not go out.

examples.ja: 暑いから、窓を開けます。
examples.reading: あついから、まどをあけます。
examples.en: Because it is hot, I will open the window.

examples.ja: 明日は休みですから、ゆっくり寝ます。
examples.reading: あしたはやすみですから、ゆっくりねます。
examples.en: Since tomorrow is a day off, I will sleep in.

questions.prompt: Choose the reason connector: 忙しい＿、行けません。
questions.explanation: The correct answer is “から”. から links being busy to the inability to go as its reason.

questions.prompt: Use a plain noun reason: 学生＿、お金がありません。
questions.explanation: A noun predicate uses だ before reason から: 学生だから.

questions.prompt: Which gives illness as the reason for resting?
questions.explanation: 病気だから places illness before から as the cause; reversing the clauses changes the causal claim.

questions.prompt: Choose the best English meaning: 暑いから、窓を開けます。
choices: Because it is hot, I will open the window.
I opened the window although it was cold.
I will open the window until it is hot.
Opening the window made it hot.
questions.explanation: “暑いから、窓を開けます。” means “Because it is hot, I will open the window.” in this example. から can give the speaker’s justification and can precede a request or decision.

questions.prompt: Choose the best English meaning: 明日は休みですから、ゆっくり寝ます。
choices: I slept in yesterday because I worked.
Tomorrow is a day off despite sleeping in.
Since tomorrow is a day off, I will sleep in.
questions.explanation: “明日は休みですから、ゆっくり寝ます。” means “Since tomorrow is a day off, I will sleep in.” in this example. から can give the speaker’s justification and can precede a request or decision.

grammar.title: Comparison with より
grammar.explanation:
A は B より adjective means A is more adjective than B. より marks the comparison baseline, not the item being evaluated.

Formation: A は B より adjective. B より A のほうが adjective also evaluates A as greater on the named scale.

Usage and cautions: より marks the baseline, not the winning item. The adjective determines what “more” means: 安い is cheaper, not more expensive. To ask between two choices use AとBとどちらが… . Unlike English, Japanese does not add a comparative suffix to the adjective.

examples.ja: 電車はバスより速いです。
examples.en: The train is faster than the bus.

examples.ja: 今日は昨日より寒いです。
examples.reading: きょうはきのうよりさむいです。
examples.en: Today is colder than yesterday.

examples.ja: この本はあの本より安いです。
examples.reading: このほんはあのほんよりやすいです。
examples.en: This book is cheaper than that book.

questions.prompt: In AはBより高い, which is more expensive?
choices: The sentence does not compare anything
questions.explanation: The correct answer is “A”. A is the topic being described; B is the comparison baseline.

questions.prompt: Say “My older brother is taller than me”: 兄は私＿背が高いです。
questions.explanation: 私より makes the speaker the comparison baseline; the predicate describes 兄 as taller.

questions.prompt: In バスより電車のほうが速い, which is faster?
questions.explanation: 電車のほうが identifies the train as the more rapid item; バスより gives the baseline.

questions.prompt: Choose the best English meaning: 今日は昨日より寒いです。
choices: Today is as warm as yesterday.
Tomorrow will be colder than today.
questions.explanation: “今日は昨日より寒いです。” means “Today is colder than yesterday.” in this example. より marks the baseline, not the winning item.

questions.prompt: Choose the best English meaning: この本はあの本より安いです。
choices: That book is cheaper than this one.
This book is cheaper than that book.
This book is more expensive than that book.
questions.explanation: “この本はあの本より安いです。” means “This book is cheaper than that book.” in this example. より marks the baseline, not the winning item.

grammar.title: Ranges: から・まで
grammar.explanation:
から marks a starting point and まで an endpoint in time or space. Both can appear together to specify a range.

Formation: Start + から + end + まで. Either endpoint can appear alone; places as well as times can form a range.

Usage and cautions: まで marks how far or how long something continues. までに instead gives a deadline by which a bounded action must occur. Do not translate English “by Friday” with まで if you mean a submission deadline rather than a continuing activity.

examples.ja: 九時から五時まで働きます。
examples.en: I work from nine to five.

examples.ja: 駅から学校まで歩きます。
examples.reading: えきからがっこうまであるきます。
examples.en: I walk from the station to the school.

examples.ja: 店は十時から八時まで開いています。
examples.reading: みせはじゅうじからはちじまであいています。
examples.en: The shop is open from ten to eight.

questions.prompt: Complete 'until Friday': 金曜日＿。
questions.explanation: The correct answer is “まで”. まで gives the endpoint; から would mean starting from Friday.

questions.prompt: Choose the starting point: 月曜日＿金曜日まで働きます。
questions.explanation: 月曜日から gives the beginning of the work period; 金曜日まで gives its end.

questions.prompt: Choose a deadline: 金曜日＿レポートを出してください。
questions.explanation: までに means submit by Friday; bare まで would describe continuation rather than this submission deadline.

questions.prompt: Choose the best English meaning: 駅から学校まで歩きます。
choices: I stay at the station until school ends.
I go from home to the station by bus.
I walk from the station to the school.
I walk from the school to the station.
questions.explanation: “駅から学校まで歩きます。” means “I walk from the station to the school.” in this example. まで marks how far or how long something continues.

questions.prompt: Choose the best English meaning: 店は十時から八時まで開いています。
choices: The shop is closed all day.
The shop is open from ten to eight.
The shop is open only at eight.
The shop closes at ten and opens at eight.
questions.explanation: “店は十時から八時まで開いています。” means “The shop is open from ten to eight.” in this example. まで marks how far or how long something continues.
